analysis.one_liner: Forces the Interior Department to immediately resume oil and gas leasing on federal land and offshore waters.
analysis.headline: Introduced by 9 Republican senators, the bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee the day it was filed and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the Interior Department to immediately resume quarterly oil and gas lease sales on federal land, issue leases from a 2021 Gulf of Mexico sale, and approve a new five-year offshore plan with at least 10 sales — all at lease terms locking in a 12.5% royalty rate and $2-per-acre minimum bids. It also would have barred the president from pausing or canceling federal energy leasing without Congress's approval. It went nowhere after its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain guaranteed access to federal land and offshore waters: quarterly onshore sales resuming immediately, with at least 70% of nominated parcels offered; Gulf of Mexico Lease Sale 257 leases issued within 30 days; remaining 2017–2022 offshore sales finished by the end of 2023; and a 2022–2027 offshore program with at least 10 sales, with public comment periods shortened or waived to hit the deadline. All of this at locked-in minimum terms of a 12.5% royalty and $2-per-acre minimum bids. Supporters argued drivers would benefit through more fuel supply, though new federal leases take years to produce oil.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Department to immediately resume quarterly onshore oil and gas lease sales and to offer at least 70% of parcels nominated for development under the applicable land-use plans.
Locks in minimum federal lease terms for five years: a 12.5% royalty rate, a $2-per-acre minimum bid, and annual rents of $1.50 per acre for the first five years of a lease.

Requires leases from the November 2021 Gulf of Mexico Lease Sale 257 to be issued within 30 days, requires all remaining sales from the 2017–2022 offshore program by the end of 2023, and mandates a 2022–2027 offshore program with at least 10 lease sales.
Lets the Interior Department limit or waive public comment periods and other requirements under the offshore leasing law in order to approve the 2022–2027 program by June 30, 2022.

Prohibits the president from pausing, canceling, or delaying federal energy leasing through executive action without Congress's approval, and creates a presumption that such an attempt violates the law.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would collect less for oil and gas taken from land and waters they own, since the bill locks in a 12.5% royalty rate and $2-per-acre minimum bids — terms set as floors rather than subject to market bidding above them. Communities near new onshore and offshore drilling would bear the local environmental effects, and the public comment process for offshore plans could be shortened or waived. The executive branch would lose its authority to limit leasing for climate or environmental reasons.

drawbacks.text: The bill fixes onshore lease terms at a 12.5% royalty and $2-per-acre minimum bids for five years, rates long criticized as below what states charge on their own land, meaning the public would collect comparatively little for resources it owns.

It removes the executive branch's ability to pause or scale back federal leasing — including pausing new leasing under Executive Order 14008 on the climate crisis — and requires replacement sales within three years if any sale is delayed.

It would let the Interior Department cut short or waive public comment periods and other requirements of the offshore planning law to meet a June 30, 2022 deadline, reducing public input on where drilling occurs.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that most new federal leases take years to explore and produce, so the bill's price-relief case for 2022's high gasoline prices is weak, while the access and low-royalty terms it grants to industry are immediate and lasting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated case — that resuming leasing would ease 2022's high energy prices — rests on a slow lever: new federal leases generally take years to produce oil. Its immediate effects run the other way for the public: below-market royalty and bid floors on resources taxpayers own, short-circuited public comment on offshore drilling plans, and a permanent bar on executive-branch authority to limit leasing. For the oil and gas industry, the benefits are direct and substantial; for ordinary people, the near-term benefit is speculative and the costs are concrete.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. John Barrasso introduced the bill on May 17, 2022, with six colleagues listed on the original text, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
Eight Republican senators had signed on as cosponsors by the end of the Congress; no Democrat did.
The Energy and Natural Resources Committee never held a markup or vote, and the full Senate never considered the bill; the only action in its entire history is the initial referral.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and all bills not enacted, including this one, expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil and gas industry gained nothing beyond what existing law already allowed, since none of the bill's mandated sales, locked-in low lease terms, or limits on presidential authority took effect. Decisions about the pace of federal leasing stayed with the administration and the regular leasing laws.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal leasing policy stayed with the administration

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wyoming (ranking member, Energy and Natural Resources Committee); bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Lease Now Act of 2022 to force immediate resumption of federal oil and gas leasing.

for.name: 8 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Lummis, Risch, Marshall, Hoeven, Cruz, and Hyde-Smith
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no additional action followed.

against.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, leaving it parked at referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Republicans and none of the chamber's 48 Democrats or 2 independents signed on; with no vote ever held, the partisan split shows only in sponsorship and in the Democratic chair's decision not to advance it.

industries.note: The bill mandates quarterly onshore lease sales, requires offering at least 70% of nominated parcels, and locks in low lease terms — a 12.5% royalty and $2-per-acre minimum bids — giving companies guaranteed, below-market access to publicly owned minerals while barring executive limits on leasing. Industry gain comes directly at the expense of federal revenue and leasing flexibility.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling companies (Gulf of Mexico and Alaska)
industries.note: The bill forces issuance of Lease Sale 257 leases within 30 days, requires all remaining 2017–2022 offshore sales by the end of 2023, and mandates at least 10 sales in the 2022–2027 program — while allowing public comment periods to be shortened or waived to meet the deadline.
